question: A 55-year-old woman with bilateral symmetric hand joint swelling, morning stiffness lasting over one hour, and positive anti-CCP antibodies has been taking ibuprofen for 6 months. Her pain improves but her joints remain swollen and progressively deformed. What is the MOST important change to her treatment?

answers.text: Start a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) such as methotrexate

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. This patient has rheumatoid arthritis (bilateral symmetric involvement, prolonged morning stiffness, positive anti-CCP). NSAIDs relieve pain and stiffness but do NOT prevent joint destruction — only DMARDs (methotrexate is first-line) modify the disease course by suppressing autoimmune pannus formation. Delaying DMARD initiation leads to irreversible erosion.

answers.text: Switch to a more potent NSAID such as indomethacin

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Switching to a stronger NSAID will not address the fundamental problem. In RA, joint destruction is driven by autoimmune pannus formation, which no NSAID — regardless of potency — can suppress. A DMARD (methotrexate) is essential to modify the disease course.

answers.text: Add paracetamol to improve her analgesic response

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Adding paracetamol provides additional pain relief but does not address the ongoing autoimmune joint destruction in RA. The critical unmet need is disease modification with a DMARD, not more analgesia.

answers.text: Continue ibuprofen at a higher dose and reassess in 3 months

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Continuing NSAIDs alone while RA remains active is a serious management error. Every month of untreated RA allows further autoimmune-mediated joint erosion. Methotrexate should be started without delay — the 'window of opportunity' for preventing irreversible damage narrows with time.

overallFeedback.feedback: In RA, NSAIDs address symptoms but NOT the underlying autoimmune process. DMARDs — methotrexate is first-line — are essential to suppress pannus formation and prevent progressive joint erosion. The principle: treat RA early and aggressively with disease-modifying agents.

Excellent. The key distinction: OA is managed symptomatically (analgesics, NSAIDs, ultimately joint replacement), while RA requires early DMARD therapy (methotrexate first-line) to prevent irreversible autoimmune joint destruction.
